title: Symmetric Polynomials and the Fundamental Theorem of Symmetric Functions

items.title: Symmetric polynomials as the invariants of variable permutations
The symmetric polynomials form a subring
items.strategy: Every variable permutation fixes zero and one and commutes with addition, additive inverses, and multiplication. Thus the common fixed set is a subring. Include the zero-variable ring as the base ring itself.

items.title: The elementary symmetric polynomials $e_0,e_1,\ldots,e_n$
Vieta expansion: $\prod_{i=1}^n(t-x_i)=\sum_{k=0}^n(-1)^k e_k t^{n-k}$
items.strategy: Expand the product and group terms by the subset of variables from which the negative term was selected. A subset of size $k$ contributes sign $(-1)^k$, its variable product, and $t^{n-k}$. Check $n=0$ as the empty-product identity.

items.title: Vieta's formulas identify the coefficients of a split monic polynomial with elementary symmetric functions of its roots
items.strategy: Substitute the roots into the universal expansion and compare coefficients to obtain $a_k=(-1)^k e_k(\alpha_1,\ldots,\alpha_n)$. Retain roots with multiplicity and handle the monic constant polynomial.

items.title: Monomial symmetric polynomials indexed by partitions
Monomial symmetric polynomials form an $R$-basis of the symmetric-polynomial ring
items.strategy: Partition monomials into permutation orbits. Symmetry makes coefficients constant on an orbit, yielding a finite combination of orbit sums. Distinct orbit sums have disjoint monomial supports, giving uniqueness without dividing by orbit sizes.

items.title: Lexicographic order on exponent tuples and the multidegree of a nonzero polynomial
The leading multidegree of a symmetric polynomial is weakly decreasing
items.strategy: If the greatest exponent tuple has $a_i<a_j$ for some $i<j$, swapping variables $i$ and $j$ produces a monomial with the same nonzero coefficient and a lexicographically larger tuple, a contradiction.

items.title: The leading multidegree of $e_1^{b_1}\cdots e_n^{b_n}$ is $(b_1+\cdots+b_n,b_2+\cdots+b_n,\ldots,b_n)$ with coefficient one
items.strategy: The leading monomial of $e_k$ is $x_1\cdots x_k$. Multiply these monic leading terms and record that the cumulative-sum map from $b$ is injective.

items.title: Every symmetric polynomial over a commutative ring is a polynomial in the elementary symmetric polynomials
items.strategy: For leading tuple $a_1\ge\cdots\ge a_n$, subtract the leading coefficient times $e_1^{a_1-a_2}\cdots e_n^{a_n}$. The leading term cancels and the multidegree decreases. Well-founded lexicographic induction terminates; treat zero and $n=0$ separately.

items.title: The elementary symmetric polynomials are algebraically independent over the coefficient ring
items.strategy: In a nonzero formal relation choose the term with maximal cumulative-sum multidegree after $T_k\mapsto e_k$. Those leading multidegrees are distinct and monic, so the selected nonzero coefficient cannot cancel, even over a ring with zero divisors.

items.title: Fundamental theorem of symmetric polynomials: unique expression as a polynomial in $e_1,\ldots,e_n$
items.strategy: Combine lexicographic existence with algebraic independence for uniqueness, and state the resulting $R$-algebra isomorphism.

items.title: A symmetric polynomial in the roots of a monic polynomial is a unique polynomial in its coefficients and lies in the base ring
items.strategy: Write it uniquely as $Q(e_1,\ldots,e_n)$ and replace each elementary value by the signed coefficient from Vieta. This is independent of root ordering.

items.title: Power sums $p_k$ and complete homogeneous symmetric polynomials $h_k$
The generating-series identity $E(-t)H(t)=1$
items.strategy: Compare each coefficient in $\prod_i(1-x_it)\sum_{k\ge0}h_kt^k$. The calculation is finite in each degree and may equivalently be organized by cancellation among monomials.

items.title: The complete homogeneous symmetric polynomials $h_1,\ldots,h_n$ freely generate the symmetric-polynomial ring
items.strategy: Coefficient comparison expresses each $h_k$ as $(-1)^{k-1}e_k$ plus earlier terms and conversely expresses $e_k$ triangularly in the $h_i$. The inverse triangular substitutions transfer generation and algebraic independence.

items.title: Newton's identities: $k e_k=\sum_{i=1}^k(-1)^{i-1}e_{k-i}p_i$
items.strategy: Differentiate the finite product $E(-t)=\prod_j(1-x_jt)$ formally, multiply coefficientwise by $H(t)$, and compare the coefficient of $t^{k-1}$. No logarithms or division are used. Take $e_0=1$ and $e_k=0$ for $k>n$.

items.title: If $n!$ is invertible, then $p_1,\ldots,p_n$ freely generate the symmetric-polynomial ring
items.strategy: Invertibility of $n!$ makes $1,\ldots,n$ units. Newton's identities recursively solve for each $e_k$ in the power sums. The triangular unit-diagonal change of variables also gives algebraic independence. State the field corollary for characteristic zero or greater than $n$.

items.title: The Vandermonde polynomial $\Delta_n=\prod_{i<j}(x_i-x_j)$
The square of the Vandermonde polynomial is symmetric
items.strategy: A permutation reindexes the unordered pairs of variables. In $\Delta_n^2=\prod_{i<j}(x_i-x_j)^2$, reversing the orientation of a pair has no effect, so every permutation fixes the product. This direct square argument includes characteristic two.

items.title: The discriminant of a monic polynomial as the coefficient expression of $\Delta_n^2$
The discriminant is $\prod_{i<j}(\alpha_i-\alpha_j)^2$ and vanishes exactly when a monic polynomial has a repeated root
items.strategy: Evaluate the defining coefficient polynomial in a splitting field. In a field the product vanishes exactly when two roots coincide, in every characteristic. Translate this into the published repeated-root criterion.

items.title: The monic resultant $\operatorname{Res}(f,g)$ from the symmetric coefficient expression of $\prod_i g(x_i)$
For monic $f$, $\operatorname{Res}(f,g)=\prod_i g(\alpha_i)$ and it vanishes exactly when $f$ and $g$ have a common root
items.strategy: The product in formal roots is symmetric, so its elementary expression defines the resultant from coefficients. Vieta evaluation yields the root product. For positive-degree $f$ over a field, it vanishes exactly when some root of $f$ is a root of $g$, including $g=0$.

items.title: For monic $f,g$ of degrees $n,m$ splitting in a common extension, $\operatorname{Res}(f,g)=\prod_{i=1}^n\prod_{j=1}^m(\alpha_i-\beta_j)$
items.strategy: Write $g(x)=\prod_{j=1}^m(x-\beta_j)$ in the common splitting extension and substitute this factorization into $\operatorname{Res}(f,g)=\prod_{i=1}^n g(\alpha_i)$. If either degree is zero, both sides are the same empty product.

items.title: For monic $f,g$ of degrees $n,m$, $\operatorname{Res}(f,g)=(-1)^{mn}\operatorname{Res}(g,f)$
items.strategy: Take a splitting field of $fg$ and apply the double-root product in both orders. Replacing every factor $\alpha_i-\beta_j$ by $-(\beta_j-\alpha_i)$ contributes one minus sign for each of the $mn$ pairs.

items.title: For monic $f$, if $g-g_1=qf$, then $\operatorname{Res}(f,g)=\operatorname{Res}(f,g_1)$
items.strategy: At every root $\alpha_i$ of $f$, evaluation of $g-g_1=qf$ gives $g(\alpha_i)=g_1(\alpha_i)$. The two root-product formulas are therefore equal, including the zero-degree and zero-polynomial boundary cases.

items.title: For monic $f$ of degree $n$, $\operatorname{Res}(f,f')=(-1)^{n(n-1)/2}\operatorname{Disc}(f)$
items.strategy: At each root, differentiate the split product to obtain $f'(\alpha_i)=\prod_{j\ne i}(\alpha_i-\alpha_j)$. Multiplication pairs every difference with its negative, one sign per unordered pair, and comparison with the root formulas gives the identity.

title: Symmetric Polynomials and the Fundamental Theorem of Symmetric Functions — Examples

items.title: Reducing a symmetric polynomial in two variables to a polynomial in $e_1$ and $e_2$
items.strategy: Run the leading-term subtraction algorithm on $x^3+y^3+x^2y+xy^2$, recording each lexicographic decrease and verifying the final expression.

items.title: The lexicographic reduction algorithm in three variables
items.strategy: Use a symmetric polynomial with several orbit types, subtract the prescribed elementary monomial at each leading partition, and verify the resulting expression by expansion.

items.title: A fixed unbalanced one-variable substitution need not preserve lexicographic leading terms
items.strategy: Give two exponent tuples for which the lexicographically larger one receives the smaller weighted exponent under a poorly chosen fixed weight list. Explain why degree-dependent separated weights can work but do not replace the lexicographic proof.

items.title: Newton's identities through $p_4$ in three variables
items.strategy: Write the identities for $k=1,2,3,4$, with $e_4=0$, solve for the first four power sums, and over characteristic zero invert $1,2,3$ to recover the elementary generators.

items.title: Power sums need not generate the symmetric ring in characteristic two
items.strategy: In two variables over $\mathbb F_2$, $p_1=e_1$ and $p_2=e_1^2$. Thus polynomials in $p_1,p_2$ lie in $\mathbb F_2[e_1]$ and cannot equal the independent generator $e_2$.

items.title: Complete homogeneous symmetric polynomials and their recurrence in two variables
items.strategy: Compute $h_0,h_1,h_2,h_3$, verify $h_k=e_1h_{k-1}-e_2h_{k-2}$, and express $e_1,e_2$ back in terms of $h_1,h_2$.

items.title: The discriminant of $x^2+bx+c$ and its double-root criterion
items.strategy: Use roots and Vieta to compute $(\alpha-\beta)^2=b^2-4c$. Check vanishing versus a repeated root in every characteristic, while separating the characteristic-two completed-square issue.

items.title: The discriminant of $x^3+px+q$ is $-4p^3-27q^2$
items.strategy: Apply the resultant-with-derivative identity or reduce the Vandermonde square by Vieta. Establish the integer polynomial identity before specializing to any field.

items.title: Computing the monic resultant of two quadratics from roots and coefficients
items.strategy: For $f=x^2+ax+b$ and $g=x^2+cx+d$, reduce $g(\alpha)g(\beta)$ using Vieta, display the coefficient formula, and test cases with and without a common root.

title: Algebraic Extensions, the Degree of an Extension, and Finite Fields

items.title: The degree $[K:F]=\dim_F K$ of a finite field extension
A finite extension has degree one if and only if the two fields are equal
items.strategy: If the degree is one, the nonzero vector $1$ is a basis, so every element of $K$ is a scalar multiple of $1$ and lies in $F$. Conversely $F/F$ has basis $\{1\}$.

items.title: Products of bases form a basis in a tower of finite extensions
items.strategy: For bases $u_1,\ldots,u_m$ of $K/F$ and $v_1,\ldots,v_n$ of $L/K$, expand first in the $v_j$ and then each coefficient in the $u_i$ to prove spanning by $u_iv_j$. Reverse coefficient comparison to prove independence.

items.title: Tower law for finite extensions: $[L:F]=[L:K][K:F]$
items.strategy: Choose finite bases for $K/F$ and $L/K$. Their products form a basis of $L/F$ indexed by the Cartesian product, so its size is the product of the two sizes. All displayed degrees are finite-dimensional degrees.

items.title: The degree of an intermediate field divides the degree of a finite extension
items.strategy: For $F\subseteq K\subseteq L$ with $L/F$ finite, obtain finite bases for the subextensions from finite spanning sets and apply $[L:F]=[L:K][K:F]$.

items.title: Every finite field extension is algebraic
items.strategy: If $[K:F]=n$, then $1,a,\ldots,a^n$ are $n+1$ vectors in a space spanned by an $n$-element basis and are dependent. The resulting nontrivial relation is a nonzero polynomial over $F$ vanishing at $a$.

items.title: An element is algebraic over $F$ if and only if its simple extension $F(a)/F$ is finite
items.strategy: The forward implication is the published quotient-and-power-basis theorem. The reverse implication applies finite-implies-algebraic to $F(a)/F$ and selects $a$.

items.title: Finitely generated field extensions $F(a_1,\ldots,a_r)$
An extension generated by finitely many algebraic elements is finite
items.strategy: Build the tower obtained by adjoining one generator at a time. Each step is finite because its generator stays algebraic over the larger base. Repeatedly apply the tower law; the empty generating list has degree one.

items.title: The elements of an extension algebraic over the base field form a subfield
items.strategy: For algebraic $a,b$, the field $F(a,b)$ is finite over $F$. Its elements, including $a-b$, $ab$, and $a^{-1}$ when $a\ne0$, are algebraic. Verify zero and one and apply the subfield criterion.

items.title: The relative algebraic closure of $F$ in an extension $K$
Algebraicity is transitive in towers of field extensions
items.strategy: For $a$ algebraic over $K$, take one polynomial over $K$ that it satisfies. Its finitely many coefficients generate a finite extension $M/F$; adjoining $a$ is finite over $M$. The tower law makes $M(a)/F$ finite, hence $a$ algebraic over $F$.

items.title: The relative algebraic closure of $F$ in $K$ has no further algebraic elements inside $K$
items.strategy: If $A$ is the subfield of elements algebraic over $F$ and $b\in K$ is algebraic over $A$, then $A(b)/A$ and $A/F$ are algebraic. Transitivity makes $b$ algebraic over $F$, so $b\in A$.

items.title: For finite subextensions in a common field, $[EE':F]\le [E:F][E':F]$
items.strategy: Products of bases of $E/F$ and $E'/F$ span the generated ring. Algebraicity reduces inverses by minimal polynomials, so this ring is the compositum. Extract a basis from the product spanning set to obtain the bound.

items.title: The prime subfield as the intersection of all subfields
The characteristic of a field is zero or a prime number
items.strategy: The characteristic is not one. If a positive characteristic $n$ were composite, write $n=ab$ with $1<a,b<n$. Minimality makes $a1_F$ and $b1_F$ nonzero, while their product is $n1_F=0$, contradicting the domain property.

items.title: A field's prime subfield is isomorphic to $\mathbb Q$ in characteristic zero and to $\mathbb F_p$ in characteristic $p$
items.strategy: In characteristic $p$, map $[n]$ in $\mathbb Z/p$ to $n1_F$. In characteristic zero, extend the injective integer map by $a/b\mapsto(a1_F)(b1_F)^{-1}$. Each image is a subfield contained in every subfield.

items.title: The binomial theorem over an arbitrary commutative ring
items.strategy: Induct on $n$. Multiply the previous expansion by $x+y$, reindex the two finite sums, and use Pascal's identity. Coefficients are repeated additions, never quotients, so positive characteristic is included.

items.title: A prime $p$ divides $\binom pk$ for $0<k<p$
items.strategy: Use $k\binom pk=p\binom{p-1}{k-1}$. Since $p$ does not divide $k$, Euclid's lemma forces $p$ to divide the binomial coefficient. Keep the endpoint coefficients outside the claim.

items.title: Frobenius $x\mapsto x^p$ is an injective endomorphism in characteristic $p$, and an automorphism for finite fields
items.strategy: The ring binomial theorem gives $(x+y)^p=x^p+y^p$ because the intermediate coefficients vanish. Powers give multiplicativity. The kernel is zero in a field; on a finite field injectivity gives bijectivity. The $n$-fold iterate is $x\mapsto x^{p^n}$.

items.title: Finite fields and their order
Every finite field has order $p^n$ for a unique prime characteristic $p$ and positive integer $n$
items.strategy: The prime subfield has $p$ elements. The finite underlying set spans the field over it and contains a basis of size $n\ge1$. Coordinates identify the field with the functions from an $n$-set to a $p$-set, hence it has $p^n$ elements. Record uniqueness.

items.title: The multiplicative group $\mathbb F_q^\times$ of a finite field is cyclic
items.strategy: A field is an integral domain and its nonzero elements are its units. Apply the published theorem that every finite subgroup of a domain's unit group is cyclic to the whole finite unit group. Its proof already supplies the root-bound and finite-abelian-structure argument.

items.title: In characteristic $p$, the roots of $x^{p^n}-x$ form a subfield and are all simple
items.strategy: Iterated Frobenius proves closure under subtraction and multiplication; zero and one are roots, and inverses follow from $a^q=a$. The derivative is $qx^{q-1}-1=-1$, so the roots are simple. Require $n\ge1$.

items.title: For every prime $p$ and $n\ge1$, a field with $p^n$ elements exists
items.strategy: Take a splitting field of $x^{p^n}-x$ over $\mathbb F_p$. Its roots form a subfield and generate the splitting field, hence are the whole field. Simplicity and the degree show that there are exactly $p^n$ roots.

items.title: A field with $q$ elements is the splitting field of $x^q-x$ over its prime subfield
items.strategy: Cyclicity gives $a^{q-1}=1$ for every nonzero $a$, and zero also satisfies $a^q=a$. Thus all $q$ elements are roots of the degree-$q$ polynomial, and they generate the field.

items.title: Finite fields of the same order are isomorphic
items.strategy: Two fields of order $q=p^n$ have isomorphic prime subfields and are splitting fields of $x^q-x$ over them. Transport the base copy and apply splitting-field uniqueness. Do not claim the isomorphism is unique.

items.title: The subfields of $\mathbb F_{p^n}$ are the unique fields $\mathbb F_{p^d}$ for positive divisors $d$ of $n$
items.strategy: A subfield has order $p^d$ and the tower law forces $d\mid n$. Conversely the roots of $x^{p^d}-x$ inside $\mathbb F_{p^n}$ form a subfield with $p^d$ elements when $d\mid n$. Any subfield of that order has the same root set.

items.title: Over $\mathbb F_q$, $x^{q^n}-x$ is the product of all monic irreducibles whose degrees divide $n$
items.strategy: In the splitting field, an irreducible of degree $d$ contributes roots exactly when their simple extension is the subfield with $q^d$ elements, equivalent to $d\mid n$. The derivative is $-1$, so factors occur once. Normalize them to be monic.

items.title: For every finite field $\mathbb F_q$ and every $n\ge1$, a monic irreducible polynomial of degree $n$ exists
items.strategy: Choose a generator of $\mathbb F_{q^n}^{\times}$. If its minimal polynomial had degree $d<n$, the element would lie in a subfield with at most $q^d-1$ nonzero elements, contradicting its order $q^n-1$.

items.title: Every finite extension of a finite field is simple
items.strategy: Coordinates make the extension finite as a set. A generator of its cyclic multiplicative group, together with zero, lies in and exhausts the subfield it generates.

items.title: Algebraically constructible real numbers as the smallest real subfield closed under positive square roots
A real number is algebraically constructible exactly when it lies in a finite tower of real quadratic adjunctions
items.strategy: The union of all finite towers from $\mathbb Q$ obtained by adjoining positive square roots is a subfield: combine two towers by appending their generators. It is square-root closed, and minimality gives equality with the constructible field.

items.title: An algebraically constructible real algebraic number has degree over $\mathbb Q$ equal to a power of two
items.strategy: Place the number in a finite quadratic tower. The top degree is a power of two by the tower law, and the simple subextension degree divides it. Unique prime factorization makes that divisor a power of two.

items.title: The real cube root of two is algebraic but not algebraically constructible
items.strategy: Eisenstein at $2$ makes $x^3-2$ irreducible, so the simple extension has degree three. Since three is not a power of two, the constructible-degree obstruction applies.

title: Algebraic Extensions, the Degree of an Extension, and Finite Fields — Examples

items.title: $\mathbb Q(\sqrt2)/\mathbb Q$ has degree two
items.strategy: Prove $x^2-2$ irreducible and apply the simple-extension theorem for basis $1,\sqrt2$ and degree two. Display two-coordinate arithmetic.

items.title: $\mathbb Q(\sqrt[3]{2})/\mathbb Q$ has degree three
items.strategy: Eisenstein at $2$ proves irreducibility of $x^3-2$. The quotient-and-power-basis theorem gives basis $1,a,a^2$.

items.title: $\mathbb Q(\sqrt2,\sqrt3)$ has degree four and equals $\mathbb Q(\sqrt2+\sqrt3)$
items.strategy: Use the tower law and compare coordinates to get degree four. For $a=\sqrt2+\sqrt3$, compute $a^{-1}=\sqrt3-\sqrt2$ and recover both roots. Verify the four-element product basis.

items.title: The relative algebraic closure of $\mathbb R$ in $\mathbb C$ is all of $\mathbb C$
items.strategy: Every $a+bi$ satisfies the nonzero real polynomial $(x-a)^2+b^2$, so every complex number is algebraic over the reals.

items.title: $\mathbb F_4=\mathbb F_2[t]/(t^2+t+1)$ with complete addition and multiplication tables
items.strategy: Check the quadratic has no root in $\mathbb F_2$, list $0,1,a,a+1$, reduce by $a^2=a+1$, compute both tables, and verify the three nonzero elements form a cyclic group.

items.title: $\mathbb F_8=\mathbb F_2[t]/(t^3+t+1)$ and its power table
items.strategy: Test zero and one to prove the cubic irreducible, list the eight power-basis elements, reduce by $a^3=a+1$, and compute powers through $a^7=1$.

items.title: $\mathbb F_9=\mathbb F_3[t]/(t^2+1)$ and a generator of its multiplicative group
items.strategy: Check that $-1$ is not a square in $\mathbb F_3$, list the nine elements, and find an element of order eight. Contrast it with the residue class of $t$, which has order four.

items.title: Frobenius on $\mathbb F_4$ swaps the two non-prime-field elements
items.strategy: Rebuild $\mathbb F_4$ as $\mathbb F_2[t]/(t^2+t+1)$ and write $a$ for the residue class of $t$. Using $a^2=a+1$, compute the squares of all four elements. Frobenius fixes $\mathbb F_2$, exchanges $a$ and $a+1$, and its square is the identity.

items.title: The subfields of $\mathbb F_{64}$ have orders $2,4,8,64$
items.strategy: Since $64=2^6$, apply the lattice theorem to divisors $1,2,3,6$ and identify each unique subfield as a Frobenius root set.

items.title: The residue class of $t$ generates $\mathbb F_8^\times$
items.strategy: Rebuild $\mathbb F_8$ as $\mathbb F_2[t]/(t^3+t+1)$ and write $a$ for the residue class of $t$. Reduce powers by $a^3=a+1$ to show $1,a,\ldots,a^6$ are the seven distinct nonzero elements and $a^7=1$. No primitive-root definition from the other run batch is used.

items.title: An algebraic extension need not be finite
items.strategy: Inside $\mathbb R$, take the union of $\mathbb Q(2^{1/2^m})$. Every element lies in a finite algebraic stage, but the stage degrees $2^m$ are unbounded; a finite total degree would be divisible by all of them.

items.title: There is no field with six elements
items.strategy: A finite-field order is a prime power, and six is no positive power of any prime. A six-element ring may exist, but not a field.

items.title: FALSE: $\mathbb F_{p^n}$ is the ring $\mathbb Z/p^n\mathbb Z$
items.strategy: For $p=2,n=2$, the finite-field existence theorem supplies a field with four elements, while $\mathbb Z/4\mathbb Z$ has the nonzero nilpotent class $[2]$ and is not a field. Equal cardinality does not determine ring structure.

items.title: FALSE: degrees add in a tower of finite field extensions
items.strategy: Use $\mathbb F_2\subset\mathbb F_4\subset\mathbb F_{64}$. The step degrees are two and three, while the total degree is six, not five; the tower law gives the product.
